item.title: Copper price sinks into bear market, erasing 2026 gains in worst week of the year
item.description: AI’s pull on copper was “a bit over-egged”, says Benchmark, and the metal piled up in the US on tariff bets is now being shipped to China, where traders are paying $500 premiums.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Copper price sinks into bear market, erasing 2026 gains in worst week of the year AI’s pull on copper was “a bit over-egged”, says Benchmark, and the metal piled up in the US on tariff bets is now being shipped to China, where traders are paying $500 premiums.

Staff Writer | November 20, 2026 - 12:29 pm

Categories: Markets

Stock image.

Copper slumped again on Friday, tipping the metal into a bear market just ten weeks after it set an all-time high, as the unwinding of bets on the artificial intelligence boom, a strong dollar and fading US tariff prospects continued to swamp evidence of acute shortage in China.

Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, dropped as much as 3.4% to $5.4405 a pound ($11,994 a tonne), the lowest since the end of March, before recovering to $5.4995 around midday, down 2.4%. That is 20.2% below the record settlement of $6.8885 reached on September 9. A close under $5.51 would meet the common definition of a bear market, a fall of 20% or more from the most recent peak.

The contract has fallen for seven sessions in a row and is down more than 9% since last Friday, by far its steepest weekly loss of 2026. A year-to-date gain that stood at 22% in September has turned into a loss of 2%, and copper is on course to end November about 15% lower.

On the London Metal Exchange, three-month copper fell 2.3% to $12,235 a tonne in official trading after touching $12,020, the lowest since March 24, Reuters reports. The benchmark is down about 9% on the week, its biggest weekly fall since early April 2025, when US President Donald Trump unveiled his global tariffs. London copper is 18% below its September 10 peak of $14,875 and would have to drop under $11,900 to join New York in a bear market. In Shanghai, futures racked up their worst week in 15 years, according to Bloomberg.

Next stop, the March low

The break below $5.63, where copper ended 2025, removes the first of two chart supports that Saxo Bank’s Ole Hansen flagged during Wednesday’s rout . The second is $5.32, which sits just beneath the lowest close of 2026: $5.34 on March 20, when surging oil prices during the Iran war and swelling exchange inventories sent the metal to a three-month trough. Copper is now less than 3% above that level.

Evidence is mounting that the AI investment boom is waning and that the Federal Reserve will have to get more aggressive to control inflation, Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, told Reuters, adding that a strengthening dollar is also weighing on the metal. AI shares continued to sag on Friday, with Anthropic trading about 9% below Thursday’s close after its market debut, the news agency said.

“We have been saying for as long as AI has been driving the price that this might be a bit over-egged,” Albert Mackenzie, copper analyst at Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, told Bloomberg. Weak Chinese demand, the dimming prospect of US tariffs and the dollar are also at work, and the week’s losses are not far off the slumps seen in the early stages of the pandemic and after Trump’s Liberation Day announcement. London copper is heading for its steepest monthly decline since 2022 .

Metal heads to China

The selloff in futures is still running alongside a scramble for physical metal in China. The Yangshan premium paid to import copper into the country slipped to $495 a tonne on Friday from Thursday’s record $500, Reuters reports. It was $360 on Wednesday and less than $100 in September. Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks rose by 3,204 tonnes this week to 30,846 tonnes, which is still less than a day’s worth of Chinese consumption.

That tightness may be part of what is pushing futures down. Premiums at these levels have made it profitable to move metal out of the United States, where stockpiles ballooned over the past year on tariff bets, and traders have begun shipping copper from the US to China , with tens of thousands of tonnes due to arrive in January. Codelco is meanwhile offering Chinese buyers 2027 cathode at $250 to $280 a tonne , less than it charged this year.

The flow looks set to continue. China’s refined copper imports are poised to climb in 2027 after a rare drop this year, according to a Reuters poll of 15 analysts and traders, because shortages of concentrate and scrap are holding back domestic smelter output while demand keeps growing. Imports fell 16% to 2.37 million tonnes in the first ten months of 2026, the lowest for the period since at least 2015.

“The gravitational pull of refined copper is now towards China,” said Nicholas Snowdon, head of metals and mining research at Mercuria, although Argus expects a moderate recovery rather than a surge.

In London the squeeze has eased: cash copper was at only a slight premium to the three-month contract on Friday after flipping into a discount earlier in the week.

$127 billion in a week

Copper stocks were sold again in New York. Eleven of the largest copper-exposed miners have lost a combined $127 billion, or 15% of their market value, since last Friday, and $208 billion, or 23%, over the past month. Their combined worth has dropped to $696 billion from $769 billion on Wednesday morning.

Freeport-McMoRan fell another 5.4%, taking its loss for the week to 22% and cutting its market value to $67 billion, from close to $100 billion a month ago. Southern Copper gave up 4.3% to $116 billion and has shed 32% in a month, a slide that has pushed the stock into the red for 2026 after it was up 41% in mid-October.

BHP was little changed at $177 billion but is down 14% on the week, and Rio Tinto eased 1.3% to $127 billion. Glencore, at $71 billion, has lost a fifth of its value in a month. Teck Resources dropped 3.6% to $24 billion, Antofagasta 4.8% and First Quantum Minerals 3.7%, and Lundin Mining’s 2.3% decline left it 19% lower since last Friday.

Only BHP, Glencore, Teck and Anglo American are still showing gains for the year, and Anglo’s is down to 1%. Ivanhoe Mines has lost 60% in 2026.

(With files from Reuters and Bloomberg)

item.title: Copper price craters as AI, tariff trades unwind, wiping $186 billion off top producers in a month
item.description: Stan Druckenmiller has gone short and Asia Copper Week heard that demand is ‘recessionary-like’, yet Chinese buyers are paying a record premium for prompt metal.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Copper price craters as AI, tariff trades unwind, wiping $186 billion off top producers in a month Stan Druckenmiller has gone short and Asia Copper Week heard that demand is ‘recessionary-like’, yet Chinese buyers are paying a record premium for prompt metal.

Staff Writer | November 18, 2026 - 8:58 am

Categories: Markets

Credit: Adobe Stock

Copper plunged to its lowest since April on Wednesday as speculators abandoned bets tied to the artificial intelligence boom, a surging dollar and fading US tariff prospects overwhelmed signs of acute physical shortage in China, and the loss of key chart levels added to momentum selling, dragging shares of the biggest producers down by between 5% and 9%.

Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, fell as much as 6.7% to $5.5835 a pound ($12,309 a tonne) in late morning trade, the lowest since early April, and more than 82,000 contracts had changed hands by midday. The contract has fallen for five sessions in a row and at the day’s low was down 16% in three weeks and 19% below the record settlement of $6.8885 reached on September 9. A gain for 2026 that stood at 22% at the peak has been wiped out, with the price dipping below where it ended last year.

On the London Metal Exchange, three-month copper was down 3.4% at $12,772.50 a tonne in official trading and later extended its loss to as much as 5.6%, the lowest since April, Bloomberg reports. In Shanghai the most-traded contract shed 3.4% to 97,920 yuan ($14,690) a tonne, and tin, the other metal most closely tied to AI hardware, slumped more than 7% in London to its lowest in almost eight months.

Underlying consumption is not helping either. “Copper demand today is closer to a recessionary-like environment than growth environment,” Nicholas Snowdon, head of metals and mining research at Mercuria, told the World Copper Conference Asia in Shanghai on Wednesday, according to Bloomberg. Natixis analysts have described the combination of US stockpiling and AI-linked investment flows as a bubble, while banks remain split on whether 2027 brings shortage or surplus .

Miners routed

The selling spread to equities as the session wore on. Eleven of the largest copper-exposed miners lost a combined $49 billion, or more than 6% of their market value, by early afternoon in New York, taking their losses to $112 billion over the past week and $186 billion, or 20%, over the past month.

BHP dropped 6.5% to a market value of $178 billion, $32 billion less than a month ago and well under the $207 billion it was worth during last week’s short-lived bounce . Southern Copper has been hit hardest among the majors, down 5.2% on the day and 26% in a month to $125 billion, a loss of $45 billion that has cut its 2026 gain to 6% from 41% in mid-October. Freeport-McMoRan, worth about $100 billion a month ago, fell 6.7% to $74 billion and is barely positive for the year.

Rio Tinto lost 5.1% to $130 billion and Glencore 6.5% to $72 billion, while Anglo American fell 8.0% and Teck Resources 7.4%. Antofagasta and Lundin Mining were the day’s worst performers among the larger names, both down more than 9%, and along with Rio are now in negative territory for 2026.

First Quantum Minerals, which jumped on Tuesday after Panama opened formal talks on restarting Cobre Panama , fell 5.5% and is 23% lower over the month. Ivanhoe Mines has shed 34% in a month and 58% in 2026.

Towel thrown in

Investors appear to be giving up after the loss of several technical levels added to momentum selling, Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank, told Reuters, pointing to an inflation scare and the risk of higher funding costs. “AI was a trigger, but it’s not really the driver,” he said.

Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities, described the move to Bloomberg as a complete recalibration of the copper market: worries about Federal Reserve tightening are weighing on the demand outlook, the midterm results have dented optimism about AI spending, and the New York premium over London, a proxy for tariff expectations, is narrowing. Speculative positioning has largely unwound and in places flipped net short, while selling by trend-following funds has accelerated the decline, McKay said.

Tech stocks steadied on Wednesday after Nvidia reported a 103% jump in quarterly revenue to $115.8 billion late on Tuesday, the chipmaker’s first results since Jensen Huang’s exit rattled the metals demand story , but that did nothing for copper. The dollar is holding near a 19-month high ahead of the release of minutes from the Federal Reserve’s October meeting, at which two officials voted for another rate increase.

Sentiment took a further knock late on Tuesday when Stan Druckenmiller, among the best-known backers of copper’s AI trade, told a conference in Austin he is now short the metal. A filing earlier in the week showed his family office had sold out of Southern Copper and bought gold miners during the third quarter.

Druckenmiller exits copper, steel and chip stocks to buy gold miners

Fund positioning has already been cut hard. Managed money net long positions on Comex have fallen from more than 80,000 contracts six weeks ago to about 35,000, close to a 14-month low, according to Saxo. Hansen put the next chart supports at $5.63 and $5.32 a pound. The first of those, which is also where copper ended 2025, gave way later in the session.

Record premium, falling price

The rout comes with the physical market in China as tight as it has been in years. The Yangshan premium paid to import copper into the country jumped by about a fifth to a record $360 a tonne on Wednesday, Reuters reports, up from less than $100 in September. Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks dropped 18% last week to 27,642 tonnes, the lowest since December 2023, and the November contract expired on Monday at a premium of more than $2,000 a tonne to December, a squeeze that forced the exchange to intervene .

Investors increasingly doubt the Trump administration will press ahead with tariffs on refined copper after this month’s midterm elections, and the spike in Chinese prices has created the commercial case for traders to ship metal out of the United States, where warehouses hold roughly 85% of the 1.09 million tonnes in exchange-monitored stocks. The assumption that those inventories would stay stranded unless tariffs were formally ruled out has been shaken, Bloomberg reports.

Supply news ignored

Chile’s copper commission Cochilco expects national output to fall 8.4% this year to 4.94 million tonnes, the lowest in 23 years , after production dropped 8.5% to 3.63 million tonnes in the first nine months. The country’s leaching operations are also exposed to sulphuric acid supply: imports hit a record 3.97 million tonnes last year, about half of consumption, and China supplied 37% of that before restricting exports in May.

In Shanghai, where the industry has gathered for annual supply talks, China’s Nonferrous Metals Industry Association said concentrate-fed smelting capacity has nearly reached a ceiling and promised a monitoring mechanism to bring treatment charges back to sustainable levels. Spot charges sank to a record minus $247.20 a tonne on November 6, meaning smelters pay miners for the privilege of processing their concentrate.

The 2026 benchmark was set at zero, and 21 of 35 industry participants polled by Reuters expect a negative number for 2027, with forecasts from minus $50 to minus $150. Snowdon argued that the more negative the benchmark, the healthier the market in the long run. Freeport Indonesia is meanwhile offering 2027 cathode from its Manyar smelter to Chinese buyers at a premium of $158 a tonne, Reuters reports, citing two sources.

The MINING.COM TOP 50 ranking of the world’s most valuable miners had already lost $226 billion in October.

item.title: Brazil pushes back on EU review of Anglo American nickel deal
item.description: Brazil disputes Brussels' authority over a Chinese acquisition as Anglo American warns its two nickel mines could close.
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Jamasmie
item.content:encoded:
Brazil pushes back on EU review of Anglo American nickel deal Brazil disputes Brussels' authority over a Chinese acquisition as Anglo American warns its two nickel mines could close.

Staff Writer | November 18, 2026 - 3:43 am

Categories: Critical Minerals Top Companies

Barro Alto. ( Image courtesy of Anglo American | Flickr. )

Brazil has challenged the European Union’s scrutiny of Anglo American’s (LON: AAL) $500-million sale of its Brazilian nickel operations to China’s MMG (HKE: 1208), raising concerns about foreign regulators intervening in domestic mining transactions.

Brazil’s foreign ministry wrote to the European Commission, the EU’s antitrust regulator, arguing that the deal involves Brazilian assets and falls outside its jurisdiction, Reuters reported. The Commission is reviewing whether MMG could redirect ferronickel supplies from Europe to China, potentially hurting European stainless steel producers.

“If the transaction is prohibited, Anglo American will place Barro Alto and Codemin (mines) into care and maintenance, with closure as the objective. This is not a negotiating position,” Anglo American CEO Duncan Wanblad wrote last week to executives at ferronickel customers including Acerinox (BME: ACX), Aperam (AMS: APAM) and Outokumpu (HEL: OUT1V).

The dispute highlights growing tensions between national control over critical minerals and foreign competition oversight, as governments seek to protect strategic resources and industrial supply chains. Brazil has identified nickel as a priority mineral because of its economic and geopolitical importance, while European authorities are seeking to safeguard supplies for domestic manufacturers.

Sovereignty concerns

Brazil’s competition regulator, Cade, has not opposed the transaction. A European Commission spokesperson confirmed contact with Brazilian authorities but declined further comment.

Brazilian mining industry association Ibram has joined the EU investigation as an interested third party. Its head of institutional affairs, Pablo Cesario, warned that the review could set a precedent for foreign intervention in transactions involving Brazilian assets.

EU scrutiny of Anglo-MMG nickel deal tests China stance

The challenge comes as Brazil strengthens oversight of its mineral sector. The country’s newly established National Council for the Industrialization of Critical and Strategic Minerals has placed nickel among its priorities, reflecting efforts to retain greater influence over resources important to industrial development.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva had planned to raise the dispute with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at a climate conference in Turkey, but the meeting did not take place.

Supply risks

MMG has offered assurances that ferronickel deliveries to European customers would continue after the acquisition, seeking to address concerns about potential supply disruptions.

The proposed takeover puts Anglo American’s efforts to divest its Brazilian nickel assets at odds with European competition concerns, leaving the future of the operations dependent on regulatory approval.

The European Commission is scheduled to decide on the transaction by Dec. 21.

(With files from Reuters)
